rows.answer: Mutual funds may avail intraday borrowing for unitholder pay‑outs such as redemptions, IDCW pay‑outs and interest, for pay‑ins related to investments made by the scheme, for mark‑to‑market obligations and foreign‑exchange settlements, for repayment of existing borrowings, and, as per Regulation 42(1), solely to meet redemption and other pay‑outs to unitholders[1][2][4].
The intraday borrowing conditions in the July 10, 2026 circular become effective on September 1, 2026[3][1].
The cost of intraday borrowing, if any, shall be borne by the Asset Management Company (AMC) [1].

No, a mutual fund may not borrow more than twenty per cent of the net assets of a scheme; borrowing is capped at 20% of the scheme’s net assets and any excess is prohibited【4】. An exception exists for intraday borrowing, which is not subject to the 20% cap provided the board‑specified conditions are met【4】.

The risk‑ometer for mutual fund schemes displays six risk levels – Low risk, Low to Moderate risk, Moderate risk, Moderately High risk, High risk and Very High risk – each associated with a specific colour (Irish Green, Chartreuse, Neon Yellow, Caramel, Dark Orange and Red respectively) [2]. These levels correspond to risk‑value ranges as follows: ≤ 1 = Low, > 1 to ≤ 2 = Low to Moderate, > 2 to ≤ 3 = Moderate, > 3 to ≤ 4 = Moderately High, > 4 to ≤ 5 = High and > 5 = Very High [3].
A Large Cap Fund must invest at least 80% of its total assets in large‑cap stocks.[6][5]
An open‑ended scheme must have at least 20 investors, and no single investor may hold more than 25 % of the scheme’s corpus.[1]
The certification examination for mutual fund distributors is conducted by the National Institute of Securities Markets (NISM) [1].

The Master Circular for Mutual Funds identified as HO/24/13/11(1)2026‑IMD‑POD‑1/I/7602/2026, issued on 20 March 2026 and effective from 1 April 2026, is the circular presently in force, superseding the earlier Master Circular dated 27 June 2024.[1][3]
The Master Circular for Mutual Funds identified as SEBI/HO/IMD/DF2/CIR/P/2020/156, issued on 24 August 2020 and effective from 24 August 2020, was the applicable master circular in January 2021.[1]
Not found in the loaded documents.
A Large Cap Fund must invest at least 80% of its total assets in large‑cap stocks. [1][6]

The July 10 2026 circular superseded the earlier guidelines on borrowings of mutual funds – specifically the provisions in clause 5.9.1 of the SEBI Master Circular for Mutual Funds dated 20 March 2026 and SEBI Circular HO/(92)2026‑IMD‑POD‑2/I/7885/2026 dated 25 March 2026.[1]

The Gazette Notification dated July 3 2026 (CG‑MH‑E‑07072026‑274229) amended the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 to permit intraday borrowings by mutual funds for various purposes as specified in the circular.[2]
The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 replaced the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996.[1][2]
The Master Circular issued on March 20, 2026 replaces the earlier Master Circular for Mutual Funds dated June 27, 2024.[1]
